Terms used in this journal
Model and parameters
The model is the program being trained. Parameters are the adjustable numbers it learns; more parameters do not by themselves prove better skills.
Token and tokenizer
A token is a piece of text, which may be a word, part of a word, or punctuation. The tokenizer decides how to split text into these pieces.
Valid label or target
A next-piece prediction the training or scoring rules actually count. Some positions are excluded, so processed input tokens and valid targets can differ.
Update and checkpoint
An update changes the model after some training examples. A checkpoint saves the model and, when available, the state needed to resume training.
Loss and perplexity
Two measures of text-prediction error. Lower is better on the same test under the same rules. Neither is a reasoning score or has a universal passing mark.
Development panel and holdout
A development panel is a fixed set used while making decisions. A sealed holdout is kept aside for a final check. Repeated development checks are not fresh final tests.
Baseline, control, and transfer
A baseline or control is a reference for a comparison. Transfer means a learned skill still works when the task or setting changes.
Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)
Training on example answers or actions after, or instead of, general text training. Fit to those examples is separate from success on new requests.
Protocol, tool, and receipt
A protocol sets the required output format. A tool is an action the surrounding software can run. A receipt records a tool result, but does not prove it acted on the right object.
Guard and budget
A guard enforces limits such as time or storage. Passing a guard check is evidence about the software, not the model’s intelligence. Reserved work and completed work are different counts.
BF16 and FP32
Number formats used for computation and stored state. FP32 keeps more precision. Different calculation settings can affect whether measurements are strictly comparable.
Hash and provenance
A hash is a fingerprint of exact file contents. Provenance records where data or a model came from. These help trace evidence; they do not by themselves prove quality or rights.

The question

Original · 3 — jump to plain-language version

Was there a usable starting point for a small training experiment, and which assumptions still needed evidence?

In plain language · 3 — back to original

Could this machine support a small training experiment, and what still needed checking?

Original · 4 — jump to plain-language version

A hardware specification alone would not answer that question. GPU memory could already be allocated, the active Python interpreter might lack a compatible framework, and nominal storage capacity might not provide a writable workspace. The method was a bounded, read-only inventory of the operating system, device driver, memory accounting, storage, and selected software availability.

In plain language · 4 — back to original

The hardware specifications were not enough. GPU memory might already be in use, Python might lack suitable training software, and available storage might not be writable. We made a limited inspection of the operating system, driver, memory, storage, and selected software without changing them.

The software checks had a deliberately limited conclusion: the checked host interpreter did not have PyTorch. They did not establish that every possible virtual environment or container lacked it. Likewise, a GPU visible to the operating system was not yet evidence that PyTorch could execute on it.

In plain language · 6 — back to original

We established only that this particular Python environment lacked PyTorch. Other environments or containers might have it. Seeing a GPU in the operating system did not yet show that PyTorch could use it.

Memory accounting mattered

Original · 7 — jump to plain-language version

Linux reported 30.48 GiB of system memory, with approximately 27 GiB available. The GPU driver reported a 32 GiB VRAM budget, of which roughly 31.44 GiB was allocated. Only about 575 MiB remained in that GPU allocation pool.

In plain language · 7 — back to original

Linux reported 30.48 GiB of system memory, with about 27 GiB free. The GPU had a reported 32 GiB allocation budget, but about 31.44 GiB was already assigned. Only about 575 MiB remained in that pool.

Original · 8 — jump to plain-language version

Reported GPU activity was 0% at the snapshot. That did not make the allocated memory available for training: idle computation and free memory are different conditions.

In plain language · 8 — back to original

The GPU reported 0% activity at that moment. A processor can be idle while its memory is still reserved, so idle did not mean ready for training.

Original · 9 — jump to plain-language version

The driver also reported a 15.24 GiB GTT budget. This overlaps system RAM and must not be added to the other figures as extra physical memory. The Linux and VRAM split was consistent with a 64 GB configuration, but the physical capacity was not independently verified. Reading firmware memory information was denied by the operating system's permissions, and the inventory did not use elevated privileges.

In plain language · 9 — back to original

The driver also reported 15.24 GiB of GTT, a pool that overlaps system memory. It is not extra memory to add to the totals. The split looked consistent with a 64 GB machine, but we did not independently verify physical memory. The operating system denied access to firmware memory details, and we did not seek higher privileges.

Original · 10 — jump to plain-language version

Storage had sufficient apparent headroom for a small diagnostic, but a writable training-data location was still undecided. Capacity and permission were treated as separate checks.

In plain language · 10 — back to original

Storage appeared large enough for a small test, but we had not chosen a writable place for training data. Free capacity and permission to write were separate questions.

Failures and unresolved observations

Original · 11 — jump to plain-language version

The failed PyTorch import was a useful result: a functioning GPU driver was insufficient on its own, and a compatible software environment would have to be established before testing the model.

In plain language · 11 — back to original

The failed PyTorch load was useful evidence. A working GPU driver alone was not enough; we needed compatible training software before testing the model.

Original · 12 — jump to plain-language version

An initial notebook-generation wrapper also failed with a Python syntax error before reaching the remote system. It made no remote changes and was corrected before the notebook was created.

In plain language · 12 — back to original

The first script for creating the notebook failed with a Python syntax error before reaching the remote machine. It changed nothing there and was fixed before the notebook was created.

Original · 13 — jump to plain-language version

At this stage, the source of the large GPU memory allocation had not yet been established conclusively. The setup work did not attempt to free that memory. The later diagnostic entry records the memory release and the environment that actually passed the tests.

In plain language · 13 — back to original

We did not yet know for sure what held the GPU memory, and this setup phase did not try to free it. The later diagnostic post records releasing memory and the environment that passed tests.

What remained to decide

Original · 14 — jump to plain-language version

The proposed model still lacked a settled architecture, tokenizer, licensed training corpus, training budget, and evaluation design. The next engineering steps were to make GPU capacity available, choose an isolated software environment, and test a tightly bounded workload before projecting a longer run.

In plain language · 14 — back to original

We still needed to choose the model design, text-splitting rules, licensed training text, budget, and tests. Next came freeing GPU capacity, choosing an isolated software environment, and trying a small, limited workload before estimating a longer run.

Original · 15 — jump to plain-language version

This inventory established a starting point and its uncertainties. It produced no trained model and no evidence of language-model quality.

In plain language · 15 — back to original

A token is a piece of text, which may be a word, part of a word, or punctuation. The tokenizer decides how to split text into these pieces.
Valid label or target

Update and checkpoint
An update changes the model after some training examples. A checkpoint saves the model and, when available, the state needed to resume training.
Loss and perplexity
Two measures of text-prediction error. Lower is better on the same test under the same rules. Neither is a reasoning score or has a universal passing mark.
Development panel and holdout
A development panel is a fixed set used while making decisions. A sealed holdout is kept aside for a final check. Repeated development checks are not fresh final tests.
Baseline, control, and transfer
A baseline or control is a reference for a comparison. Transfer means a learned skill still works when the task or setting changes.
Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)

A protocol sets the required output format. A tool is an action the surrounding software can run. A receipt records a tool result, but does not prove it acted on the right object.

Terms used in this journal
Model and parameters
The model is the program being trained. Parameters are the adjustable numbers it learns; more parameters do not by themselves prove better skills.
Token and tokenizer
A token is a piece of text, which may be a word, part of a word, or punctuation. The tokenizer decides how to split text into these pieces.
Valid label or target
A next-piece prediction the training or scoring rules actually count. Some positions are excluded, so processed input tokens and valid targets can differ.
Update and checkpoint
An update changes the model after some training examples. A checkpoint saves the model and, when available, the state needed to resume training.
Loss and perplexity
Two measures of text-prediction error. Lower is better on the same test under the same rules. Neither is a reasoning score or has a universal passing mark.
Development panel and holdout
A development panel is a fixed set used while making decisions. A sealed holdout is kept aside for a final check. Repeated development checks are not fresh final tests.
Baseline, control, and transfer
A baseline or control is a reference for a comparison. Transfer means a learned skill still works when the task or setting changes.
Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)
Training on example answers or actions after, or instead of, general text training. Fit to those examples is separate from success on new requests.
Protocol, tool, and receipt
A protocol sets the required output format. A tool is an action the surrounding software can run. A receipt records a tool result, but does not prove it acted on the right object.
Guard and budget
A guard enforces limits such as time or storage. Passing a guard check is evidence about the software, not the model’s intelligence. Reserved work and completed work are different counts.
BF16 and FP32
Number formats used for computation and stored state. FP32 keeps more precision. Different calculation settings can affect whether measurements are strictly comparable.
Hash and provenance
A hash is a fingerprint of exact file contents. Provenance records where data or a model came from. These help trace evidence; they do not by themselves prove quality or rights.

# Model Training Journal

An AI-assisted engineering journal about training a small language model from scratch. Public entries distinguish observed results from plans, preserve failures and limitations, and omit private operational details.

Read the journal at **https://obra.github.io/model-training-journal/**.

## Structure

- `content/posts/`: curated public Markdown entries with title, date, slug, phase and summary front matter.
- `content/`: experiment index, editorial method, reviewed dashboard additions and hash-bound plain-language companions.
- `templates/` and `assets/`: shared HTML and restrained, responsive styling.
- `scripts/`: local builder and publication checks.
- `docs/`: generated static HTML served by GitHub Pages from `main`.

No notebook mirror, raw logs, model weights, dataset copies or credentials belong in this repository.

## Build

```sh
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
.venv/bin/python scripts/build.py
```

The build is local and deterministic. It uses no CDN, remote fonts or tracking.
The only browser JavaScript is the reviewed local snapshot-age and cutoff clock;
charts are static SVG images. The generated pages are committed so they can be reviewed before publication. GitHub Pages serves `main:/docs` with `.nojekyll`.

See [PUBLISHING.md](PUBLISHING.md) for the review-and-publish procedure. Publication needs an existing authorized GitHub login; this project neither creates nor transfers credentials.

## Rights and provenance

The entries summarize project observations and cite external sources. No third-party dataset or text excerpt is distributed. Software and data license observations in articles describe the original experiment; they are not a license grant for external materials. Do not add copied material without verifying and recording redistribution rights.

## Reader access and measurements

Every post pairs the original with a plain-language companion. The homepage and
[dashboard](https://obra.github.io/model-training-journal/dashboard/) share one
compiled evidence model. See [the schema and update guide](scripts/dashboard-README.md)
for correspondence checks, missing-data rules and adding future measurements.
